source.title: Simplicity bias and optimization threshold in two-layer ReLU networks

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; minor PDF/OCR formatting artifacts do not prevent reading the relevant sections.
record.tranche_reason: The paper explicitly distinguishes its sample-size behavior from data double descent and reports that test loss decreases rather than rises as training sample size increases.
record.gate_note: The paper tests sample-size behavior using test-loss results, including a theoretical excess-risk statement. It does not sweep model size or test error over training epochs. Neuron-alignment cosines and training-loss-only results are not rows for the versions because they do not measure the test-error shape.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps training-set size for overparametrized two-layer networks (m = 10 000) trained to convergence with label noise. It reports test loss across the point where the network stops interpolating, so it bears on V3 in a new setting: small-initialization feature learning on toy regression. Appendix B states its test loss falls monotonically with n, unlike data double descent. It neither runs nor reanalyses the original sweeps and makes no argument that V3 is wrong, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but the main conclusion is different. The authors' central claim is that overparametrized ReLU networks with small initialization fail to reach a global minimum once n exceeds an optimization threshold. They converge instead to a simple, near-OLS solution, and this simplicity bias improves generalization. The contrast with data double descent (monotone test loss in n) is a side remark in Appendix B.
record.recipe_differences: This paper analyzes and experimentally studies a two-layer network's optimization threshold and sample-size behavior, rather than reproducing the original double-descent sweeps over model size, epochs, or data size.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported transition varies with dimension and teacher complexity: for d = 10 the OLS-like behavior begins at larger sample sizes, and the 5-ReLU teacher transitions more slowly than the linear teacher. The reported GeLU and Adam variants also show similar behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: Beyond an optimization threshold in n, overparametrized ReLU networks stop interpolating and converge to a spurious stationary point near OLS. Training loss rises toward σ² while test loss approaches the optimum.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small-initialization feature learning, more data induces an optimization threshold past which networks no longer interpolate; this improves test loss rather than producing a sample-wise peak.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The empirical sample-size results are primarily presented as plots, without reported error bars or uncertainty estimates. The experiments use toy two-layer networks and limited data settings; the authors note the theoretical assumptions are restrictive.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted. The main Figure 2, GeLU Figure 4, Adam Figure 5, d = 10 Figure 7, and 5-ReLU-teacher Figure 8 test-loss sweeps are recorded. Training-loss curves and Figure 3 neuron-alignment cosines do not measure the test-error behavior named by the claim.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep; width is fixed at m = 10 000. Figure 1 is a schematic.
No test-error trajectory over epochs; only test loss at convergence is reported.
There is no fine-grained n sweep near n ≈ the parameter count; n stays far below m(d+1). No settings with larger models, real data or large initialization.
No capacity sweep across model classes.
No effective-complexity measure is used to predict peak location.
No noise-level sweep, no regularization tuning and no multiple-peak analysis.

missing.what: The authors' explicit statement contrasting their result with data double descent: test loss decreases monotonically in the number of training points.

record.verdict_notes: V3 is an existence claim ('can raise'), so a setting with no peak limits its scope rather than challenging it. The original sample-wise peak sits where n is near the model's effective capacity. Here n stays far below the raw parameter count, though the optimization threshold plays an analogous role. The theoretical rate (r1) covers only n ≥ n⋆ and is a cited OLS bound.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep of test error or peak near the interpolation size.
No test-error trajectory over training epochs.
The paper varies sample size and reports test-loss behavior, but does not narrowly map a local peak around the interpolation threshold or test this across general settings.
No capacity sweep across model classes testing post-interpolation descent.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across axes.
No noise-level sweep, multiple-peak analysis, or optimally tuned regularization test.
No comparison of double descent with a curve measured against an effective parameter count.

rows.locator: Section 4.2, “Improved test loss, due to overparametrization threshold”
rows.note: The authors state that excess risk decreases to 0 as the sample count grows in this fixed-dimension setting.
rows.check: The O(d/n) rate is cited from Hsu et al. (2011), applied to the OLS estimator reached at convergence. It holds only for n ≥ n⋆ = Θ(d³ log d), well past the interpolation transition, so it says nothing about test error near the threshold. Its 'reversed' state is not justified.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU network (m = 10 000)
rows.operation_detail: Varied training-set size and measured test loss at convergence.
rows.note: The text says the loss is much larger for smaller training sets and becomes close to the noise level beyond the threshold.
rows.check: 'Reversed' is the wrong state: falling test error with more data is just the absence of the V3 effect. Per Figure 2(b) and Appendix B, the loss is high before n⋆ ≈ 3000 and near σ² after, with no rise reported. The curve is figure-only and coarsely sampled.
